{{DISPLAYTITLE:Martin-Löf type theory}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}
Per Martin-Löf's intuitionistic theory of types, begun at Stockholm in 1971, made the identification of propositions with types the foundation of a whole system of mathematics, not an observation about one. Its first version was inconsistent; the versions that followed from 1972 to 1984 are predicative and have stood. This page follows that development and the proof assistants built on it, and says what Lean took from it.

== The first version and Girard's paradox ==

Martin-Löf's first theory, an unpublished Stockholm preprint of 1971, contained an axiom that there is a type of all types.<ref name="pml" /><ref name="sep">Peter Dybjer and Erik Palmgren, "Intuitionistic Type Theory", ''Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy'', first published 12 February 2016, substantive revision 23 September 2024. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory-intuitionistic/</ref> Jean-Yves Girard showed that this axiom leads to a contradiction. In the paper that replaced it, Martin-Löf describes the first version as based on the "strongly impredicative axiom that there is a type of all types", records that it had to be abandoned after Girard showed it contradictory, and thanks Girard for showing him the paradox.<ref name="ml1972">Per Martin-Löf, "An intuitionistic theory of types", written 1972 at the University of Stockholm; published in G. Sambin and J. M. Smith (eds.), ''Twenty-Five Years of Constructive Type Theory'', Oxford University Press, 1998, pp. 127–172. Copy of the 1972 text: https://archive-pml.github.io/martin-lof/pdfs/An-Intuitionistic-Theory-of-Types-1972.pdf</ref> Girard's argument encodes the Burali-Forti paradox of the largest ordinal.<ref name="sep" /> It appeared in his doctoral thesis at the University of Paris VII in 1972, which Martin-Löf cites when he states that a universe containing itself leads to a contradiction.<ref name="ml1984">Per Martin-Löf, ''Intuitionistic Type Theory'', notes by Giovanni Sambin of a series of lectures given in Padua, June 1980, Bibliopolis, Naples, 1984. Re-typeset edition: https://archive-pml.github.io/martin-lof/pdfs/Bibliopolis-Book-retypeset-1984.pdf</ref> A simplified form of the paradox was published by Antonius Hurkens in 1995.<ref name="hurkens">Antonius J. C. Hurkens, "A simplification of Girard's paradox", in ''Typed Lambda Calculi and Applications (TLCA '95)'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 902, Springer, 1995, pp. 266–278. doi:10.1007/BFb0014058</ref>

The lesson is the reason Lean has a hierarchy of universes instead of a single type of all types. It is told for the general reader at [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Why there is no type of all types|Why there is no type of all types]] and formally at [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Universes and Prop|Universes and Prop]].

== The predicative versions, 1972 to 1984 ==

The 1972 paper replaced the type of all types by a '''universe''' of small types, closed under all the ways of forming types except that it does not contain itself.<ref name="sep" /> Martin-Löf wrote there that the change was drastic: the theory no longer contained intuitionistic simple type theory, and its proof-theoretic strength should be close to that of predicative analysis.<ref name="ml1972" /> The paper was not published until 1998.<ref name="sep" />

The next published version was his paper to the Logic Colloquium held at Bristol in July 1973, printed in 1975 as "An intuitionistic theory of types: predicative part".<ref name="pml">"The collected works of Per Martin-Löf", an online archive of his papers, list of works with dates. https://archive-pml.github.io/</ref> It extended the single universe to a countable hierarchy of universes and added a uniform identity type, the type of proofs that two objects are equal.<ref name="sep" /><ref name="ml1975">Per Martin-Löf, "An intuitionistic theory of types: predicative part", in H. E. Rose and J. C. Shepherdson (eds.), ''Logic Colloquium '73'', Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics 80, North-Holland, 1975, pp. 73–118. doi:10.1016/S0049-237X(08)71945-1</ref>

At the International Congress of Logic, Methodology and Philosophy of Science at Hannover in 1979 he presented "Constructive mathematics and computer programming", published in 1982. It explained that the theory is at once a programming language and a foundation for constructive mathematics. It also introduced the extensional form of the theory, in which two objects proved equal are treated as the same for the purposes of type checking.<ref name="sep" /><ref name="ml1982">Per Martin-Löf, "Constructive mathematics and computer programming", in L. J. Cohen, J. Łoś, H. Pfeiffer and K.-P. Podewski (eds.), ''Logic, Methodology and Philosophy of Science VI'', North-Holland, 1982, pp. 153–175. doi:10.1016/S0049-237X(09)70189-2</ref>

The best-known account is the short book ''Intuitionistic Type Theory'', Giovanni Sambin's notes of lectures Martin-Löf gave in Padua in June 1980, published by Bibliopolis in 1984.<ref name="ml1984" /> In 1986 Martin-Löf reformulated the theory once more, inside a '''logical framework''' in which function abstraction and the dependent function type are the only binding operations; the encyclopedia entry calls this now the main version.<ref name="sep" />

== Propositions as types as the foundation ==

The Padua lectures distinguish a proposition from a judgement. A proposition is what logical operations combine; a judgement is an act of holding something true, such as "A is a proposition" or "A is true". A proposition is explained by saying what counts as a proof of it, much as a set is explained by saying how its elements are formed. Martin-Löf concludes that keeping the two notions apart would only duplicate them, and identifies them: a proposition is a set, and a proof is an element of it. He calls this the formulae-as-types, or propositions-as-sets, interpretation on which the theory is based.<ref name="ml1984" />

The correspondence itself was older. Curry had observed it for propositional logic in 1958, and Howard and de Bruijn extended it to predicate logic, which needs types that depend on objects.<ref name="sep" /> (For de Bruijn's part, see [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]].) What Martin-Löf added was a theory in which the correspondence is the starting point: the logical connectives and quantifiers are type formers, and a mathematical proof is a program. Lean works the same way; see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Propositions as types|Propositions as types]] and [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Terms, types and judgments|Terms, types and judgments]].

== Descendants ==

'''Nuprl.''' One of the first proof assistants for type theory was Nuprl, built by R. L. Constable and colleagues and described in their book of 1986. It is based on an extensional theory close to Martin-Löf's of 1982.<ref name="sep" /><ref name="nuprl">R. L. Constable, S. F. Allen, H. M. Bromley, W. R. Cleaveland, J. F. Cremer, R. W. Harper, D. J. Howe, T. B. Knoblock, N. P. Mendler, P. Panangaden, J. T. Sasaki and S. F. Smith, ''Implementing Mathematics with the Nuprl Proof Development System'', Prentice-Hall, 1986. ISBN 0-13-451832-2. Catalogue record: https://openlibrary.org/books/OL2715187M</ref> Gordon counts it among the systems built in the LCF manner, with ML as metalanguage.<ref name="gordon2000">Mike Gordon, "From LCF to HOL: a short history", in G. Plotkin, C. Stirling and M. Tofte (eds.), ''Proof, Language, and Interaction: Essays in Honour of Robin Milner'', MIT Press, 2000. Author's copy: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mjcg/papers/HolHistory.pdf</ref>

'''ALF and Agda.''' Ulf Norell's doctoral thesis at Chalmers in 2007 designed and implemented a new Agda, a programming language based on dependent type theory that is also a proof assistant. It cites as earlier systems the ALF proof editor of L. Magnusson and B. Nordström (1994) and the earlier Agda of Catarina Coquand and Thierry Coquand (1999).<ref name="norell">Ulf Norell, ''Towards a Practical Programming Language Based on Dependent Type Theory'', PhD thesis, Chalmers University of Technology and Göteborg University, 2007. https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~ulfn/papers/thesis.pdf</ref><ref name="agda2009">Ana Bove, Peter Dybjer and Ulf Norell, "A brief overview of Agda – a functional language with dependent types", in ''Theorem Proving in Higher Order Logics (TPHOLs 2009)'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 5674, Springer, 2009, pp. 73–78. doi:10.1007/978-3-642-03359-9_6</ref> Agda is based on the logical-framework formulation of Martin-Löf's predicative theory.<ref name="sep" />

'''The other branch.''' Coq and Lean descend instead from the Calculus of Constructions, which is impredicative; that line is followed at [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]. The encyclopedia entry notes that the Calculus of Inductive Constructions has a predicative part that follows Martin-Löf's principles.<ref name="sep" />

== What Lean took ==

Lean's logic combines the two lines. The 2015 description of Lean says that with an impredicative sort of propositions Lean's trusted kernel gives a version of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, and without one it gives a version of Martin-Löf type theory; in both cases there is a sequence of type universes, which in Lean are not cumulative.<ref name="lean2015">Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong, Jeremy Avigad, Floris van Doorn and Jakob von Raumer, "The Lean Theorem Prover (system description)", in ''Automated Deduction – CADE-25'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 9195, Springer, 2015, pp. 378–388. doi:10.1007/978-3-319-21401-6_26. Author's copy: https://lean-lang.org/papers/system.pdf</ref> The universes <code>Type 0</code>, <code>Type 1</code> and so on, each a member of the next and none of itself, follow the pattern Martin-Löf adopted after Girard's paradox in 1972 and extended in 1973. The impredicative <code>Prop</code> is the other branch's contribution.

Girard's 1972 thesis, the 1975 and 1982 papers, Hurkens's paper, the Nuprl book and the 2009 Agda overview were not opened; their details come from the publishers' records, the encyclopedia entry and Martin-Löf's own references.
